args.text: [lane-otter] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale addresses: users are sent to servers that have moved or been retired, causing failures. (2) Slow recovery: when a site fails over to a backup, clients keep using the old address until the cache expires. (3) Prolonged poisoning: if a false answer is cached, it stays in place and misleads users for longer.

[lane-otter] Idempotent retries matter because networks fail unpredictably, so a client often cannot tell whether its first request succeeded, and retrying is the only safe way to recover. If the request is idempotent (repeating it gives the same result as doing it once), a retry cannot cause harm such as a double payment or a duplicated order.

[lane-otter] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (a universally unique identifier whose first part is a timestamp) as a primary key: (1) Larger keys: it takes 16 bytes, against 4 or 8 for a plain integer, so indexes and foreign keys grow and are slower to scan. (2) Leaked timing: the embedded creation time is visible to anyone who sees the identifier, and ordering within the same millisecond is not guaranteed unless the generator handles it. It does keep inserts mostly in order, which is kinder to indexes than random UUIDs.

[lane-otter] A write-ahead log is a record that a database writes to disk before it changes its main data, so every change is saved in order first. If the system crashes, it can replay that record to restore finished work and undo unfinished work, keeping the data consistent and durable.

[lane-otter] (1) Fair comparison: if the client version changes between runs, any difference in results could come from the client rather than the system being tested, so pinning keeps the only variable the thing you are measuring. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the benchmark later and get comparable numbers, because updates to the client can change speed, defaults or behaviour without warning.

[lane-otter] Backpressure is a way for a queue to push back on whatever is sending it work when it is filling up faster than it can be emptied. The sender is slowed, paused or told to try later, which stops the queue growing without limit and running out of memory.

[lane-otter] Two ways a cron job (a timed task scheduler) can run twice: (1) the same schedule is installed on two machines, for example after scaling out or a failover; (2) a slow run is still going when the next one starts, so the runs overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or a database row, and exit quietly if another run already holds it.

[lane-otter] A tombstone is a small marker saved in place of a deleted item in a replicated store (one that keeps copies on several machines). Without it, a copy that missed the deletion could hand the old value back and bring the item to life again. Tombstones are cleared after a set time, once every copy has seen them; that period is unknown here.

[lane-otter] Two signs a test is flaky rather than properly failing: (1) it passes and fails on the same code with no changes, so re-running it gives different results. (2) It fails only sometimes in certain conditions, such as on a busy machine, in a particular order with other tests, or at certain times, which points to timing, shared state or outside services rather than a real bug. A genuine failure repeats every time.

[lane-otter] A lease-based lock gives one machine the lock for a set time, and each machine judges that time using its own clock. If one clock runs fast or slow (clock skew), the holder may think it still has the lock after the lock service has given it to someone else, so two machines work at once. Using fencing tokens (numbers that rise with each new lease) lets storage reject the older holder.
